theory.text: A prompt isn't a Google search. It isn't a terminal command either. It's closer to a brief you'd give a skilled collaborator: the more precise it is about what you want, for whom, and with what constraints, the more usable the result — without corrections. Vague prompts aren't inherently wrong, but they force the AI to invent the parts you left blank. And the invented parts are exactly what you'll end up rewriting.

A well-built prompt has four ingredients. The first is context: what you're building and where this task fits in the project. The second is the precise task: not "add authentication" but "implement Google login using Supabase Auth, redirect to /dashboard after login". The third is the constraint: tech stack, libraries already in use, and — crucially — what must not be touched. The fourth is the output format: do you want code ready to paste? A plan before implementation? A comment on each section? The AI doesn't know unless you say so.
💡 Think of the prompt as a brief for a very capable collaborator with no memory. Include the context they can't have — not just the mechanical instructions.

theory.prompt: Add a newsletter signup form. Stack: Next.js 15, Resend for emails, Zod for validation. Frontend component only — I'll handle the API route myself. Add one comment line per code section.
theory.output:
Here's the component. I used Zod for client-side validation as specified, removed any sending logic (handled by your route), and commented each section.

One thing: I didn't add a custom error message for invalid email — I can add it if you want.

theory.text: ⚠️ Not every prompt needs all four ingredients. But every missing ingredient is a decision the AI makes for you — one you might not agree with.

Short prompts work great when context is already established: inside an active session, with a specs file loaded, or for small fixes. The full anatomy is most useful when you open a new session on something non-trivial. The practical test is simple: is there anything the AI will have to invent because I didn't tell it? If yes, add it.
🔑 Four questions for every prompt that matters: what am I building, what exactly does it need to do, what can't it touch, how do I want it to respond.

exercise.prompt_template: Before sending a prompt, make sure it includes: the [BLANK] of the project, the precise task, the technical [BLANK], and the expected output format.

blanks.hint_1: What does the AI need to know about your project before it can understand what you're asking?
blanks.hint_2: Starts with 'c' — it's what's always missing from prompts written in a hurry.
blanks.explanation: The answer is 'context'. Without it, the AI doesn't know where the task fits and has to make assumptions about the surrounding project.

blanks.hint_1: What do you call the things the AI must not do, or the libraries it must use?
blanks.hint_2: Starts with 'c' — they're the boundaries within which the AI must work.
blanks.explanation: The answer is 'constraints'. Defining them explicitly — stack, libraries, what not to touch — dramatically reduces output that's incompatible with your project.

outro.recap: An effective prompt has four ingredients: context, precise task, constraints, and output format. Every missing element becomes a decision the AI makes instead of you.
outro.next_prompt: Next lesson: the first ingredient to master — giving the AI a role and changing the quality of its responses.
